articles.title: We cut the tags off in the changing room, walked out, and sold the clothes at half price to rich college kids
articles.deck: He failed eight papers out of ten and lost a year. Three friends died of overdoses. Then somebody asked him to play guitar at a prayer meeting, and he went because he had nothing else on that afternoon.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the November 2013 issue, pages 4 to 7, under the heading "How I met Jesus". Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. The opening paragraph is his own press biography as the magazine ran it. No earlier publication of this text was found anywhere, which is consistent with him having given it to the magazine directly; he is alive, working and contactable, and his confirmation should be obtained.

body.v: Sheldon Bangera is a lead worshiper, singer-songwriter, musician, producer and conference speaker from Mumbai. He has written over two hundred worship songs, many of them sung across India and abroad, and was the first Indian to write and record with Integrity Music. He is married to Anita Bangera, and they travel together speaking to young couples.
Early childhood

I grew up going to sunday school, singing church songs and winning prizes for scripture examinations. However, by the time I reached 8th and 9th grade, I started to lose interest in church and activities. The only reason I liked church is for the music. It was for church that I was trained to play the organ. Later on, I went on to pick up the guitar and learn it myself just by observing the Sunday School teacher play.

Soon, my interest in all church activities dwindled and I stopped attending church. I wanted to explore more of life and fun. After my 10th grade, I thought I had all the freedom to do whatever I want. With both my parents working and with nothing to really look forward to every afternoon, friends took prime spot in my life, and guess what, these were music lovers too. I spent a lot of time bunking lectures, playing the guitar outside the college main gate, drinking, smoking and yes, we started slipping into the consumption of drugs.
College days

I loved rock and heavy metal music, spent most of my time playing guitars for a rock band, practiced hard to get good at my guitaring and wanted to quit studies so that I could concentrate more on my music. Yet, there was nothing positive about the music we were playing. It was more about hatred, rebellion, hopelessness, giving us a hundred reasons to hate God and hate other people.
Whatever I did, I loved to give my best shot at it. So whether it was fights, music or overdosing on drugs, I was now pushing it to the max to see how much my body could take.

Obviously the money coming from home was limited and restricted. So, my friends and I would walk into the most expensive section of a shopping mall, happily chop off the RFID tags with great mastery, try them out at the changing room and then walk out with the most expensive clothing, go out and sell them at half rate to some naive rich college kid.

We spent most of our time at a friend's place doing drugs all day and night, talking about karma and why this life was so meaningless. When you're high on drugs, you love making up theories and talking out things out of reach as if they were well within your reach of comprehension. I bet that's how most of the world's theories have come out. A bunch of rebellious guys trying to give a name and build a system around their rebellion.
Getting darker

Life was getting more and more dark. I lost 3 friends to an overdose of drugs. Another very dear friend of mine was sent to rehab and couldn't come out of the influence of the harmful chemical drugs he was hooked on to. There were violent fights with parents at home where during fits of rage I would break furniture and other household items. Being uncontrollable, on multiple occasions the police had to come in to calm things down in a tough way. Life was hopeless, meaningless and with no future.

I almost came to be convinced that there was no God and that even if there was one, He was too far to help me out or simply, I was too far. I was far from church, living helpless and hopeless, mostly alone. I felt unloved, miserable and guilty that I had caused too much grief. I was heavily addicted to alcohol and drugs and found myself going alone to the bars often.
First year engineering

My getting admitted into an engineering college was a miracle by itself. With a percentage as low as 50 in my H.S.C College examinations, I realized that God was somehow answering all my parents prayers. I did get into one of the best colleges as one of the worst students.

Due to the drugs, I had lost some straight thinking and memory abilities. I was not able to sit to read or study for more than ten minutes at a stretch. So, I worked really hard but the result was, I flunked my first semester exams. I failed in 8 out of 10 papers and got a year drop. Thus, I was now at home with nothing much to do except play the guitar and surf the internet all day besides meeting friends.
Someone along the way invited me to play the guitar at a prayer meeting.
Encountering God

Playing the guitar is something I loved. Church and prayer meetings, I was allergic to. I thought it to be a boring place for boring people. However with not much thought, considering that I had nothing significant going on at that time, I decided to show up to play the guitar at that prayer meeting.

One afternoon, I smoked my cigarette and was heading to this prayer meeting. I stepped on stage, befriended by the music team all neatly dressed, and proceeded to take a corner spot. The unholiest among all holy people I thought I was.

The meeting was good. I had never seen people pray like that before. While people were praying, so many were experiencing the power of God at that moment. Some were weeping, some falling under the power of God, some had their hands lifted up. Never before had I seen a sight like this.

All of a sudden, a lady started to scream. It seemed like she was possessed by an evil spirit. The preacher ordered in the Name of Jesus, over and over again, before the lady dropped to the ground and the spirit left her.

I was still in the corner trying to make sense of what was going on. I had a huge question in my head: if the Name is so powerful, what then must the person be like? I knew that I had taken that Name for granted and that I did not believe in or trust in Him. I was now very afraid, not of the spirit but of the Lord's presence. I thought to myself, if evil spirits submit to Him, why then cannot humans like myself submit to Him?
If the Name is so powerful, what then must the person be like?
body.highlight: what then must the person be like

body.v: I was afraid of Him and I thought to myself, He has really been patient with me. He should have ideally destroyed me for what I had done to myself and others but He did not. In love, He patiently waited for me to meet Him.

While on one side I felt the fear of God, on the other side, I felt the love and mercy of God drawing me near. There was a voice I could hear inside. I was familiar with that voice but only as a background voice. But now, this voice was louder to me than all other voices. It was the voice of the Holy Spirit.

I heard him say a thousand things to me in a minute. He affirmed and reaffirmed that God loved me, that He had a plan for me, that He cared for me and how He was going to change me. For the first time in my entire life, I felt so loved and cared for.
Bowing my knee

The meeting was over and everybody had gathered for tea. But I was still there praying and talking to God. Without wasting much time, I wanted to bow my knee to this great and magnificent God. I gave Him my life and asked Jesus to forgive me of all my sin. I told him that I was giving Him my life and that He could do whatever he wanted with it. All my gifts, my talents, my guitar playing, my voice. I gave Him everything. I felt like I had received new life and that my world had changed.

I had so many questions and I suddenly felt new desires. The want to understand what's written in the bible and the need to be around godly people. God changed my desires and I now began to attend every prayer meeting possible, spending the rest of my time with people of God learning from God's word.
Music and friends were idols in my life and so I decided to run away from them as far as I could. I stopped playing the guitar and deleted all my music collection.
Starting new

All that I did for the next two months was read the bible and attend prayer meetings. I was listening to gospel music and serving as much as I could. It was so dramatic that even I could not believe that I was completely delivered from drugs and all the former habits.

Finally when I met my friends after two months, on being asked and probed, I started to tell them about this journey and how God saved me. I shared the truth about Jesus and His Lordship and how we are all going to be accountable to Him, how He loves all of us and wants for us to turn. This sharing did lead some to receive Jesus while others thought I was completely off my mind.
A new song

After an entire year, I picked up the guitar to play again. I loved to worship God and so I spent my time singing new songs to God. Very soon, I was writing songs that others could relate with and sing.

The Holy Spirit started to whisper in my ear that He would give me songs in Hindi for the nation to be blessed and touched. I hesitated because I was very poor with Hindi but in time, I felt like the words flowed from heaven and started touching many lives. My childhood dream was to be a musician and God was so gracious to use me in the area of song writing and leading others in worship.
Marriage

At one stage, being the kind of guy I was, I never thought anyone would marry me and I never knew if marriages would work especially because of the disturbance in my parent's marriage. I was against the idea of marriage, but God gradually worked on me and on my thinking and understanding in this subject.

He showed me through dreams how I was to get married to Anita with glimpses of how it would be for us. God promised me that He would use all my brokenness and broken experiences to help many young people and repair many broken homes.
Life today

Today, my wife Anita and I run a small company, a recording studio, a music school. Most of the time we are travelling either with the Sheldon Bangera Band for concerts or as a couple to teach and mentor youngsters. God has been very gracious to us in this one year of wedded life.

We are happy to serve in the local church whether it is about teaching in the weekly Bible study or helping young people meet with God. Anita has a burden for evangelism and every week shares the gospel at the nearby slums. It is overwhelming to see how God has taken our music and influence around the globe.
We are living to see a generation experience the life transforming power of Jesus Christ. If He did it for me, He can and will also do it for you.

articles.title: The candle failed in the mould and left a hole, so she filled it with orange wax and had room for one short verse
articles.deck: The verse that fitted was "I am fearfully and wonderfully made". Months later a pastor in Trivandrum reached for that candle while sitting with a couple who had been told to abort their baby.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the November 2013 issue, page 8. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. The 2013 page ended with her personal mobile number and email address, which have not been reproduced: republishing a private individual's contact details thirteen years later is a privacy exposure rather than a service to anyone.

body.v: Being a stay-at-home mother of two young children kept me on the go for a few years. However, deep down I knew that God had something greater planned for me.

As I prayed and sought the Lord, last year He showed me the technique of designing unique decorative candles embossed with Bible verses. These candles can be lit for a few hours without the melting wax overflowing onto the text. I was also able to design flowers with wax to make His word more prominent and beautiful.

I thank God that these candles have become very popular due to their uniqueness and non-availability in the market. It was early December in 2012 when I started making these candles and uploaded the pictures on Facebook. As the news about these candles spread, people started requesting them for different occasions like weddings, Christmas, New Year, birthdays, souvenirs for conferences and many more. These candles have also become a wonderful tool to share God's word as people who bought them also started gifting them to their friends from other faiths.
I was amazed and surprised to see how God could take something as simple as a candle and grant me the privilege to lift His word high and be a blessing to different events in people's lives.
The lighting ceremony

In January of this year I was asked to make a 24 inch tall candle which was to be used for a formal lighting ceremony in a Christian Businessmen's Conference. The verse printed on the candle was "You are the light of the world". As each participant in the conference was getting their candle lit from the flame of this large candle, I felt the importance of the work that the Lord had called me for, to impact the lives of people with His word.
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
The candle that failed

I am amazed at how the Lord is using these candles to be a blessing in the lives of people. A few months back, a pastor from Trivandrum said that he had received a call from a couple who were heartbroken because the doctor said that the child in the mother's womb had severe disabilities and therefore had to be aborted.

While speaking to this family, the pastor's eyes fell on the candle which he had just received as a gift and had kept on the shelf of his house. The verse on the candle was "I am fearfully and wonderfully made". Based on this word the pastor was able to minister to the couple and encourage them to have faith in God and not lose hope.

Interestingly, the design and verse on that candle had come about as a result of a failed trial. It was a plain white candle which following the trial had a large hole towards its base. To cover up this hole, I poured in some orange colour wax which I had handy at that time. I then sealed it with several layers of orange wax. Since nearly half of the candle was orange, I had very little space to print, and the only verse that could fit in that space was "I am fearfully and wonderfully made".
The only verse that could fit in that space was "I am fearfully and wonderfully made".
body.highlight: The only verse that could fit

body.v: Looking back I am reminded of how God uses the so called imperfect pieces and lifts them up to accomplish His purpose.
The unity candle

The first wedding unity candle that I made was for a lovely couple from my church. They trusted me to give them a unique unity candle with the words "And the two shall become one" (Mark 10:8) printed on it. Although I was excited about making the candle, I was also anxious to see how it would finally look, as it was to be used as part of the formal wedding ceremony and I was a novice in this field. As I prayed and worked on the candle, God gave me the guidance and wisdom to make a candle that was truly unique. Since then I have received requests for several unity candles and I am humbled to say that the Lord has enabled me to make good of the talents He has given me.

As I reflect on my journey thus far, I am amazed at how these candles have been a blessing and inspiration to many. In all this work, I thank God for giving me a very loving and supportive husband without whose help I would not have been able to achieve what I have achieved thus far.
My goal through this endeavour is to communicate Christ through arts. Although at this point it is in the form of candles, I am sure that in the future there will be more avenues.

articles.title: I moved seats because of the draught, and did not explain why. So of course they assumed it was them
articles.deck: A small thing left unsaid in a coffee shop, and what it costs at scale. Four questions worth asking before you open your mouth, and one before you keep it shut.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the November 2013 issue, page 10. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. He introduces the four questions as advice he received rather than as his own, and that framing is his.

body.v: Just recently I was in one of my favorite places working on a couple of projects. I was sitting pretty close to the door and felt the draft every time patrons came in and out. Being kind of cold natured, I decided to find a different seat.

As I gathered up my belongings I thought to myself, "I should probably say something to the two ladies sitting near me why I'm moving so they won't think they're the reason." Failing to listen to my intuition, I didn't say anything.

Sure enough one of them spoke up, "I hope we are not the reason you are moving. I hope we haven't been too loud." To which I said, "You know, I was just thinking I should probably tell you why I'm moving so you won't think you are the reason, but I decided not to."

As I thought about that brief exchange, I thought about how often this is true in life and leadership. How many times, because something was left unsaid, did it lead to hurt feelings, a misunderstanding, wrong conclusions, and numerous other unfavorable outcomes?
How many times, because something was left unsaid, did it lead to hurt feelings, a misunderstanding, wrong conclusions?
So what is it you need to say
Are you a parent? Maybe a son or daughter is developing bad habits or showing signs of disrespect.
Do you have friends? Maybe one of them is starting down a road that will only lead to painful experiences and they just don't see it.

Are you a leader? Do you have people that work for you? Maybe there is a pattern of behavior you are noticing in an employee that needs addressing. Or maybe they said or did something that you can't quite figure out why.

Are there people in your life who truly look to you for inspiration and direction? Maybe they need a word of encouragement or some prodding to get them moving in order to realize their full potential.
It's odd that I'm even writing this article because I've been one of those people who have hesitated to say something when something should have been said.
Why do we do that?

For many, they just don't like the conflict and uncomfortable conversation you're opening the door to, so you avoid it at all costs. For some, they fear rejection and think to themselves, "If I say something, they won't like me any more." For others, they simply don't care enough to muster the emotional energy it will take to engage in the conversation.
Experience has taught me, in most cases, it's better to speak up and say something rather than let things simmer and turn into something bigger than what they really are.

So here are just a few principles I'm trying to live by when it comes to speaking up. Care enough to confront. Believe that what you have to say matters and will make a difference in someone's life. Others need and want your perspective. Better to bring the matter into the open and deal with it than leave it in the dark and let it get worse.
And the other side of the coin

Now, however, before I finish this article, here is some great advice I've received on the use of our words. I share this because on the other side of the coin are those who have no trouble whatsoever expressing how they feel.
If that is you, ask yourself these four questions before you speak. Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it helpful? Is it kind?
So, make that phone call, initiate that meeting, engage in that conversation. Clear the air and keep the lines of communication open.
Ok, I've got to go. I just thought of someone with whom I need to go have a conversation.

articles.title: We cannot see faith, but we see everything because of it
articles.deck: The woman on the corner who feeds her children first and sleeps hungry. The student who sits an exam she has not read for and thinks she might just make it. If that is not faith, what is she living on?

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the November 2013 issue, page 16, under the heading "Moving Mountains". Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is the author's throughout. One correction: the opening scripture was cited as Luke 18:6 and the mustard seed saying is Luke 17:6.

body.v: If you had faith as big as a mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, "Pull yourself up by the roots and plant yourself in the sea!" and it would obey you.
Every day, when I wake up, I thank Him for all the things He has given me: a good night's sleep, a new day, a loving family, faithful friends, but most of all, for giving me faith.

Each day, I know He won't give me anything that the two of us together can't handle. I know that if there have been failures, it is so that I may learn to be better. Faith is nothing but complete trust in He who has made us.

We can't see faith; but we see everything because of it. Look around you. Doesn't all that you have seen teach you to trust Him for all that you have not seen? If He carried us through life this far, would He forsake us now? If He has moulded each one of us in His likeness, would He let go of us so easily?
We can't see faith; but we see everything because of it.
body.highlight: we see everything because of it

body.v: Not an excuse

People sometimes misunderstand faith. They believe that those who leave all to God are ones who are too lazy to do it themselves or want an excuse for not being capable enough to do it. Well, the concept has been turned on its head.

Faith is taking a step in the dark and believing that He is watching. It is what makes a person take a step towards something, not away from it. It is putting your best foot forward and knowing that it will not land in quicksand, but on solid ground.

When you know you haven't studied a day's worth of notes and yet give the exam and somewhere deep down, you know you might just make it, isn't that faith? That lady on the corner of the street who sleeps on an empty stomach after feeding her children all she could gather, what is she living on, if not faith? When you see that the precious little time you have with a sick friend is slipping through your fingers and yet you find a reason to smile and make them laugh, what are you living on, if not faith?
Faith in the right thing

Having faith is essential, but having faith in the right things is most important. Murderers, dacoits and thieves also have faith; only it is in the inefficiency of law and order enforcement, probably. That we place our trust in God is what matters. Trust Him to do not what you want, but what is right for you.

Remember the lady who touched Jesus' cloak and was healed? That's the kind of faith we're talking about. There isn't a dearth of worries or sorrows in our lives; it is not like we don't need healing. So what is stopping us from trusting in Him? Why do we doubt? Is it because Jesus is too far away? Is His cloak out of reach?

If so, start tonight. Pray. Every night when you close your eyes, thank Him for all that He has given you, thank Him for where He has brought you, but most of all, trust Him to know where He is taking you. Approach life with a smiling, a winning attitude and be equipped with faith. Like He said, even faith the size of a mustard seed will do.
May we all grow in trust and faith and be close to the Lord, always: close enough to reach out and touch His cloak.

articles.title: An American wrote the Hindi grammar that Indian Civil Service candidates had to pass their exams on, and it is still in the issue
articles.deck: Samuel Kellogg learned the language because he was posted alone to a station outside Farrukhabad with nobody to speak English to. The book he produced gave its name to forty-four years of Hindi scholarship, and it is on sale in Delhi today.

archiveMeta.editNote: The Missionary Story on page 15 of the November 2013 issue was reproduced from the entry on Kellogg by Thomas D. Ice in Mal Couch, ed., Dictionary of Premillennial Theology (Kregel, 1996), and carried Elizabeth Clayton's byline. Soft hyphens left mid-word on the original page, in Pre-diction, Pres-byterian, evangeli-zation and transla-tors, show it was pasted from a scan. Unlike the 1910 encyclopedia entry used in September, that book is in copyright. This is a new article, researched and written in September 2026. Nothing of the 1996 entry survives in it, and one claim from it has been dropped as unverifiable: no source anywhere confirms a gravestone at Landour reading "Till He Come". On the Executive Director's decision, this piece keeps to Kellogg's contribution to India and its languages and does not carry the criticism of him found in the research; see TRIAGE.md for what was set aside and why.

body.v: The standard history of Hindi grammatical scholarship divides itself into periods. One of them is called the Kellogg Era, and it runs from 1876 to 1920.

It is named for an American Presbyterian missionary who arrived in the North-Western Provinces at twenty-five, was left in sole charge of a station outside Farrukhabad with nobody to speak English to, and started taking notes.
The mother with the book

Samuel Henry Kellogg was born in 1839 at Quiogue on Long Island, the son of a Presbyterian minister. He was taught mostly at home. The detail that survives from that house is his mother teaching him Latin while she did the housework, the boy following her from room to room with the book open in his hands.

He lasted one session at Williams College before his health broke. At Princeton he graduated in 1861 ranked joint first in a class of a hundred. His mother died that same year. He finished at Princeton Seminary in 1864, was appointed a tutor in mathematics and was on a clear path to a professor's chair, and instead was ordained for India in April 1864.
A hundred and forty-five days

He sailed from Boston that December on a merchant ship carrying ice to Ceylon. On the third day out the captain was washed overboard in a cyclone. The officer who replaced him could not navigate, the crew began plotting a mutiny, and Kellogg, who had studied navigation, took the daily observations and brought the ship in himself.
The passage was supposed to take a hundred days. It took a hundred and forty-five.

He reached Calcutta in May 1865 and was posted to Barhpur, a station of the Farrukhabad Mission in what is now Uttar Pradesh, eight years after the rising of 1857 had gone through those provinces. He was left in charge alone, with what the record calls a small staff of Hindustani helpers. His own account of it is dry.
It was hard at first, but had the good result of bringing me on in the language much faster than I should otherwise have learned it.
body.attr: Samuel Kellogg, on being left alone at Barhpur
body.highlight: much faster than I should otherwise have learned it

body.v: He was preaching in the vernacular within six months. He began the notes that became the grammar in his first year.
What the book actually did

A Grammar of the Hindí Language was printed at the American Presbyterian Mission Press in Allahabad in 1876. It set out standard Hindi, Braj, and the Eastern Hindi of Tulsidas's Ramayan, and then the colloquial speech of Marwar, Kumaon, Avadh, Baghelkhand and Bhojpur. By the third edition the list had grown to include Magadhi and Maithili.

In his preface he counted what he had done: the declension and conjugation of nine or ten dialects nobody had previously written down, in a language he reckoned sixty to seventy million people spoke across more than two hundred and forty-eight thousand square miles.

The Government of India read it and prescribed it as the authority for every Indian Civil Service candidate required to pass the Hindi examination. It went into a second edition in London in 1893 and a third in 1938. Motilal Banarsidass keeps it in the issue today.

Frances Pritchett, who taught Indian literature at Columbia for decades, puts its continuing use plainly: the comparative grammatical tables are the reason anyone still opens it. If you meet an unfamiliar verb form in early verse, Kellogg is where you go.
He took Indian speech seriously when his colleagues did not
The most striking thing in the preface is how impatient he is with other foreigners.

Europeans of his generation tended to assume that Hindi could be manufactured by taking Urdu and swapping the Persian words for Sanskrit ones. Kellogg had watched them try it. The villagers, he wrote, stared at them confounded by sonorous Sanskrit terms that were less familiar than the Arabic and Persian they had replaced. He pointed out that a purity test strict enough to satisfy those men would disqualify Tulsidas and Kabir.

And in a footnote he refused the hierarchy his own title implied. Calling one form standard, he wrote, is not to suggest the others are corruptions of it. They are collateral branches of the old speech of India, and in most cases older and less changed than the standard itself.
It is not intended to suggest that all other dialectic forms are corruptions.

That is why the book is still usable. A grammarian who thought Bhojpuri and Awadhi were degraded Hindi would not have bothered to record their conjugations, and there would be nothing for a student to look up today.
He did not do it alone, and he says so. The work was compiled with pandits, and Indian scholars sat with him through the years of it, supplying the living speech he was writing down.
What it cost

His wife Antoinette died in March 1876, the year the grammar appeared, leaving four children. He broke up the house in India and took them to America, where he stayed fifteen years: a pastorate in Pittsburgh, then a chair in systematic theology at Allegheny.

He lost the chair in 1885. Some of the directors objected that his premillennial views did not sit with the seminary's teaching, and he resigned rather than fight. He went to Toronto instead, where the congregation grew from 503 to 704 under him.
In 1892, after fifteen months of letters from four separate bodies asking him, he went back to India at fifty-three to translate the Old Testament into Hindi.
Three men at Landour

The revision committee was Kellogg, an Anglican and a Congregationalist: W. Hooper of the Church Missionary Society and J. A. Lambert of the London Missionary Society. They worked at Landour above Mussoorie for seven or eight months a year across six hot seasons.

After Kellogg died, the two survivors decided not to appoint a third man. He had left such full notes that they could work from them: on almost every question that arose, they said, they were fairly sure what his view would have been, and when the two of them differed, whichever one's opinion diverged from his gave way at once. They carried the translation to completion.
The books, and a change of mind at the end
Alongside the Hindi work he wrote a commentary on Leviticus for the Expositor's Bible, published the year he died, which conservative preachers still reach for a century later.

He also wrote about Indian religion. The Light of Asia and the Light of the World, published in 1885, was a reply to Edwin Arnold's popular poem on the Buddha, and it is a polemic: the thesis is fixed before the argument begins. What is more interesting is what he thought about it afterwards.

In one of the last letters of his life he set out what he wanted to lecture on next. Hinduism in relation to Christian thought, the Arya Samaj, Brahmoism in its various schools. And he added that this time he wanted to dwell more on the points of contact than of contrast.
More on the points of contact, than of contrast.
body.attr: Samuel Kellogg, in one of his last letters

body.v: He was sixty years old and correcting himself, in a direction most men of his generation never travelled at all.
The bicycle

On 30 April 1899 he preached in the Methodist church at Mussoorie on the text that they shall not die any more. On 2 May he gave the weekly Bible reading at a friend's house, and called in on a sick colleague walking home.

On 3 May his doctor had him cycling for his health. He rode out along the terrace at his house on Landour hill, where there is an unguarded drop of about twelve feet. Nobody saw it happen. The servants heard the sound and found him already dead. He was fifty-nine, and he is buried in the cemetery on the hillside.
Four years later the Kellogg Memorial Church was built at Landour. It is still there.
So what, in 2026?

The grammar outlived the reason it was commissioned. Civil service candidates stopped needing it in 1947. Students of Braj and Awadhi did not, and that is why a book from 1876 is still on a shelf in Delhi with a current price on it.

Most of what people do disappears within a generation. This is a man who arrived somewhere at twenty-five knowing nothing of the language, was left alone with it, and decided that the thing to do was write down how people actually spoke, including nine or ten dialects nobody had thought worth recording.

He was not a linguist by training. He was a mathematics tutor who could have had a chair at Princeton. He got on a ship instead, navigated it himself when the captain went overboard, and spent the next thirty years on somebody else's language.
There is a lesson in there about what a life is for, and it is not a comfortable one. The work that lasted was not the work he was famous for at the time.

Sources: Kellogg's own preface to A Grammar of the Hindí Language (Allahabad, 1876), from the Internet Archive scan; Helen H. Holcomb, Men of Might in India Missions (1901), whose author knew him in India and hosted him in the weeks before his death; Philip Malayil's entry in the Dictionary of Christian Biography in Asia; Tej K.
